business: Loom — shared agentic ecosystem for AI coding teams
why_not: The context-switching pain is real — I run three AI agents a day and re-explaining context kills me — but I'm not handing my code and session data to a vendor I've never heard of on a launch day. The local daemon helps, but there's no track record, no audit, and no one I trust vouching for it yet. $30/seat is cheap enough; trust isn't.

I can't buy software without SSO, an audit log, and FIPS — none of that's in the pitch — and I'm not installing a new daemon from a tap I've never heard of until I see it discussed on Reddit and GitHub issues. If Loom shuts down, my team's shared context is locked in with no exit.

I'm a freelancer paying out of my own pocket, and $30/month is a recurring charge for a tool I'd open a few times a week. I hunt deals and jump to free tiers, so a seat fee feels like money down the drain when I'm solo and don't even have a team to share sessions with.

I'm a deal hunter who compares every AI tool on price per seat and bails for free tiers, so $30/seat/month doesn't clear my bar. On top of that I can't force my team onto one agent, so the shared-layer pitch doesn't land for me.

I run three-plus AI agents a day and losing context between tools is genuinely annoying, but we already pay for GitHub Copilot Enterprise and I'm not adding another $30-per-seat monthly bill for an unproven local daemon from an unknown founder. The first five humans are free, so I'd kick the tires on launch day — try, not buy.

No. I already pay for GitHub Copilot Enterprise and Cursor, I don't need another local daemon just to share context between agents, and I'm not installing a brew tap from an unknown publisher without seeing it vetted on GitHub or Reddit first.

I run three agents a day and context does get lost switching between them, but Cursor and Copilot already keep context inside my editor, so I'm not paying thirty dollars a month for a new local daemon I haven't vetted on GitHub or Reddit — I'd use the free five humans first and probably never convert.

I live in one editor and Cursor/Copilot already share context inside it. I'm not juggling enough agents across tools to justify installing another daemon, and I don't buy dev tools without checking Reddit and GitHub issues first — this is too new with no track record.

I run 3+ AI agents daily and losing context when switching tools is a real pain, but my first reaction to Loom was that a local daemon plus adapters and MCP servers is more infrastructure than I want to maintain right now — I'd rather keep paying the context-switching tax than babysit another piece of setup until it's proven dead simple.
why_yes: I run three or more AI agents every day and lose context every time I switch between them — that's a real, daily tax Loom is built to remove. The first five humans are free, so there's almost no cost to try it, and $30/seat later is a rounding error at my salary. My hesitation is that we already pay for GitHub Copilot Enterprise, so Loom has to prove it adds something Copilot doesn't rather than being another layer to manage.

I run three-plus AI agents daily and lose context every time I switch tools; Loom's shared session and skills layer fixes that exact pain without forcing my team onto one agent, and $30 a seat with the first five humans free is cheap enough to pilot.

I run three AI agents and context silos between them are real, but my first instinct is not to trust a new vendor with my code. Loom runs a local daemon on a Unix socket so nothing leaves my machine — that local-first design is exactly what earns my buy-in at $30/seat with the first five humans free.
